report:
**Conclusion:** Yes—offering HIV self-testing *in addition to* usual HIV testing services generally causes more people to test. A 2021 systematic review of 13 randomized trials found that self-testing approximately doubled testing uptake versus standard services alone (risk ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.69–2.58), with moderate-certainty evidence. Effects have been seen across several delivery routes and populations, particularly people who otherwise face barriers to clinic testing.

The result should not be overgeneralized: the benefit depends on making kits accessible (often free or low-cost) and on the target population. Also, an “extra” second kit does not necessarily increase testing further: one study comparing one versus two kits found no meaningful difference in HIV testing. Self-testing programs should include clear instructions and routes for confirmatory testing and treatment after a reactive result.

Sources:  
- https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext  
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7713313/  
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8366833/  
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11237351/
